overview: The common cold is an acute, self-limiting viral infection of the upper respiratory tract characterised by rhinorrhea (runny nose), nasal obstruction, sneezing, sore throat, and mild cough. It is the most frequent infectious illness worldwide — adults experience 2–4 colds per year and children up to 4–10 episodes annually. Although rarely serious, it causes significant disruption to daily life and may lead to secondary bacterial infections in some cases.

types.name: Rhinovirus Cold
types.description: The most common type, responsible for 50–70% of all cold cases. Causes classic runny nose, sneezing, and mild sore throat. Most prevalent in autumn and spring.

types.name: Coronavirus Cold (Seasonal)
types.description: Caused by seasonal coronaviruses (not SARS-CoV-2). Accounts for 10–15% of colds, mainly in winter. Presents with cough, sore throat, and fatigue — generally mild.

types.name: Adenovirus Cold
types.description: Can cause a more prominent sore throat and eye irritation (conjunctivitis) alongside cold symptoms. More common in children and military recruits.

types.name: RSV Cold (Respiratory Syncytial Virus)
types.description: Usually mild cold-like illness in adults and older children but can cause bronchiolitis and serious illness in infants and elderly individuals.

types.name: Parainfluenza Cold
types.description: Common cause of cold symptoms in children; can also cause croup (barking cough with hoarseness) in young children.

symptoms: Runny nose (rhinorrhea) — initially clear, may become thick and yellow-green
Sore or scratchy throat (often the first symptom)
Reduced sense of smell and taste
causes: Rhinovirus infection (most common — over 100 rhinovirus subtypes)
Spread through inhalation of respiratory droplets from an infected person
Touching contaminated surfaces and then touching eyes, nose, or mouth
risk_factors: Young age (children under 6 are most susceptible)
Weakened immune system (stress, poor sleep, malnutrition, illness)
Autumn and winter seasons — people spend more time indoors in crowded spaces
Close contact with infected individuals (school, daycare, offices)
Chronic conditions like asthma (increase risk of complications)
diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on symptoms alone (no tests needed in most cases)
Physical examination — redness of throat, nasal discharge
PCR testing — identifies specific virus type (used in research or severe cases)
Rapid antigen tests — useful to distinguish cold from flu or COVID-19 if needed
Differentiation from flu: cold has gradual onset, milder fever, and predominant nasal symptoms
Differentiation from allergies: cold has infectious contact, fever, and coloured discharge

symptom_relief: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) or Ibuprofen — for fever, headache, and sore throat pain
Decongestants (Pseudoephedrine, Xylometazoline nasal spray) — for nasal blockage; use for max 3–5 days
Antihistamines (Chlorpheniramine, Loratadine) — may reduce runny nose and sneezing
Cough syrups (Dextromethorphan, Guaifenesin) — for dry or productive cough if bothersome
home_remedies: Warm fluids — hot water with honey and lemon, herbal teas, warm soups
Steam inhalation — helps loosen nasal congestion
Honey (for adults and children over 1 year) — coats throat and reduces cough
Saline nasal drops or sprays — gentle nasal irrigation to clear congestion
Rest — allows immune system to fight infection more effectively
Adequate hydration — at least 8–10 glasses of water per day
what_to_avoid: Antibiotics — ineffective against viral infections; do not request or use them for a cold
Aspirin in children — risk of Reye's syndrome
Over-the-counter cold medicines in children under 6 — not recommended, potential side effects
Decongestant nasal sprays for more than 3–5 days — risk of rebound congestion

complications: Sinusitis — secondary bacterial infection of sinuses (persistent facial pain, coloured discharge)
Otitis media — middle ear infection (common in children)
Bronchitis — infection spreads to lower airways
Pneumonia — rare but possible in vulnerable groups
Laryngitis — inflammation of voice box causing hoarseness
Febrile convulsions in young children with high fever
prevention: Wash hands frequently with soap and water for at least 20 seconds
Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands
Maintain distance from people with cold symptoms
Cover mouth and nose when sneezing or coughing — use a tissue, then discard it
Disinfect frequently touched surfaces (phones, door handles, keyboards)
Get adequate sleep (7–9 hours) — poor sleep weakens immunity
Maintain a balanced diet rich in fruits and vegetables
Manage stress — chronic stress suppresses immune defence
Avoid close contact with others if you are sick
emergency_signs: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
High fever (above 39°C / 102.2°F) that does not reduce with medication
Fever lasting more than 3 days or returning after initially resolving
Symptoms lasting longer than 10–14 days without improvement
Severe sore throat with white patches (may indicate strep throat)
Ear pain or discharge (suggest ear infection)
Stiff neck or severe headache (rule out meningitis)

faqs.question: How long does a common cold last?
faqs.answer: A typical cold lasts 7–10 days. Some symptoms like cough or nasal discharge can persist up to 14 days. If symptoms are not improving after 10 days, see a doctor to rule out complications like sinusitis.

faqs.question: Should I take antibiotics for a cold?
faqs.answer: No. The common cold is caused by viruses, and antibiotics only work against bacteria. Taking antibiotics unnecessarily contributes to antibiotic resistance and may cause side effects. Use symptom-relieving medicines instead.

faqs.question: Is there a vaccine for the common cold?
faqs.answer: No. Because the cold is caused by hundreds of different viral strains (especially over 100 rhinovirus types), developing a single vaccine is not currently feasible.

faqs.question: How is a cold different from the flu?
faqs.answer: Cold symptoms develop gradually and are mainly limited to the nose and throat. Flu symptoms appear suddenly and are more severe — including high fever, body aches, chills, and significant fatigue. Flu also carries a higher risk of serious complications.
